_about: The Adventure Society contract board (Generators > Contracts). A board shows notices of several tiers; a team may take a contract of its own rank or lower, never higher. Notices, clients and the rest fill these placeholders: {client} {place} {monster} {item} {npc} {faction} {count} {days} {astral}. "pay" scales a type's reward; "reward" in each tier is the range in spirit coins of that tier. "boards" sets how many notices of each tier a settlement's board carries, as weights. 'bonusItems' marks bonuses that are things the party can keep: a saved contract offers to put them in the party inventory, or, for gear a player wears or wields ("gear": true), on one party member's sheet.
rule: A team may take any contract of its own rank or lower. The clerk will not hand a Silver contract to a Bronze team, however much they argue.

Iron.note: Local trouble a new team can handle: lone beasts, short roads, small favours.

Bronze.note: Real danger: packs, bandit crews, astral spaces of some size, journeys of several days.

Silver.note: Threats to whole towns: surge leaders, cult cells, monsters that Iron and Bronze teams cannot hurt.

Gold.note: Regional disasters and powers that move armies. Few teams are allowed near these.

Diamond.note: Rare beyond rumour. Posted by the Society itself, often sealed and read only at the counter.

boardDressing: The board is three layers deep in notices, and the oldest ones have yellowed and curled at the edges.
A harried clerk pins up a fresh notice, still damp with ink, and three teams lunge for it at once.
Someone has scrawled 'DO NOT TAKE' across one notice in charcoal, and nobody has removed it.
The Iron-rank section overflows; the Gold section holds only a single grim notice on red paper.
A cat sleeps on the clerk's desk, curled on top of the contract ledger, and the clerk refuses to move it.
Red pins mark urgent jobs, and today there are more red pins than usual.
An old adventurer with one arm sits by the board, offering unsolicited advice on every contract.
The board smells of lamp oil and wet wool; rain drips from the rafters onto a bucket nearby.
A notice has been torn down halfway, leaving only the reward line and a smear of blood.
The duty clerk wears spectacles thick as bottle glass and reads every notice aloud to anyone who asks.
A young Iron-rank team argues loudly over whether a delivery job is beneath them.
Several notices bear the wax seal of the Magic Society, all written in cramped, precise handwriting.
The hall is nearly empty; most teams left at dawn for a surge reported in the marshes.
A ranking chart beside the board lists the top teams this season, with one name freshly scratched out.
A boy runs between the board and the counter, selling cups of hot cider for a copper each.
A Silver-rank adventurer pins up her own notice, hiring porters, and glares at anyone who smirks.
One notice is written in three languages and decorated with a child's drawing of a monster.
The clerk stamps each claimed contract with a heavy brass seal that rattles the whole counter.
A tally board above the counter counts the days since the last Society fatality: currently two.
Fresh sawdust covers the floor where someone bled on it last night, and the clerk does not want to talk about it.
A Gold-rank adventurer walks past the board without looking at it, and the whole hall goes quiet until she's gone.
Someone has pinned a drawing of the duty clerk with horns. The clerk has signed it.
A notice in childish handwriting offers three copper pieces for finding a lost cat; four teams are pretending they aren't considering it.
The board has been moved to a new wall and nobody can find the Silver section.
An Iron-rank team is pinning a 'Members Wanted' notice beside the contracts, and it has clearly been rewritten several times.
A Magic Society scholar reads every notice through a lens and makes notes about the monsters named.
The counter is shut for lunch; a small queue of irritable adventurers waits with their claim slips.
A dog has been trained to bring claimed notices to the counter, and it is better at it than the junior clerk.
Rain has soaked the outdoor board, and the clerk is re-copying notices by hand, muttering.
Two notices have been pinned on top of each other so the reward of one sits under the job of the other.
A priest of the Church of the Hero is blessing each team that takes a contract, whether they asked or not.
Someone has scratched a tally of failed teams beside a Bronze notice. It's up to four.
The clerk is training a nervous replacement, who reads every notice twice and stamps it three times.
A merchant hovers by the board, trying to hire teams directly at a discount, and the clerk is pretending not to notice.
The hall smells of fresh bread: someone's grateful client has left a basket for the teams.

my husband says it is only a big dog. it is not a big dog. it is a {monster} and it sits on our roof. last house before {place}.

Hunters needed for a {monster} that has made its den in the old quarry at {place}. Quarrymen refuse to work until it is gone.

details: The creature is a single old male driven out of its territory by something bigger; it is hungry, wounded and reckless.
The beast dens in a collapsed root cellar on an abandoned farm, and it drags its kills there; bones are piled knee deep.
Tracks lead to a watering hole where the monster drinks at dusk; a DC 14 Wisdom (Survival) check finds a good ambush spot downwind.
There are actually two of them, a mated pair, and the second one hunts while the first is being chased.
The monster only attacks livestock wearing bells; the sound drives it into a frenzy.
A local hunter already wounded it with a poisoned arrow, so it is weakened but now attacks anything on sight.
It hunts only on moonless nights and spends the day buried in loose earth; a DC 13 Wisdom (Perception) check spots the disturbed ground.
The creature is marking territory with scratches on trees at head height; anyone who reads the marks can predict its loop.
Its den is behind a waterfall, and the noise covers the team's approach and the monster's.
Every attack happened within sight of the same lone oak; the monster uses it as a lookout.
Locals have been leaving offerings of meat at the edge of the woods, so the monster now expects to be fed there at dusk.
The monster is clever enough to double back on its own trail; a failed tracking check leads the team in a circle.
It has a monster core of a rank above its body: it is stronger than it looks and grows more dangerous each week.
Bones near the den include a Society badge from a hunter who went missing a month ago.
The beast is drawn to the smell of spirit coins, which is why it keeps attacking the tax collector's cart.
complications: A rival Iron-rank team took the same contract by clerical error and wants the kill credit.
Heavy rain has washed away the tracks; Survival checks to follow the trail are made with disadvantage.
The farmers want the beast alive to sell to a menagerie and will not help if the team plans to kill it.
The creature has young in its den, and a church warden insists they be spared.
A noble's hunting party is also after the monster and will not share the woods.
The monster has learned to avoid fire and flees whenever torches are lit.
The local lord forbids hunting on his land without a permit, and the den is on his land.
Fog rolls in every morning, giving the monster cover until noon.
A herd of skittish cattle sits between the team and the monster; panic them and the herd tramples a village fence.
A bard is following the team to write a ballad about the hunt and keeps making noise at the wrong moment.
The trail crosses into a marsh where a second, unrelated monster has its territory.
The client has set traps all over the woods without telling anyone where.
The monster's carcass is valuable, and bandits are watching the hunt so they can take it once it's dead.
A storm breaks on the first night and the team has to choose between shelter and the trail.
A grieving widow insists on coming along to see her husband's killer die.
twists: The monster is fleeing a newly opened astral space nearby, and more creatures will follow it out within a week.
The client deliberately lured the beast to a rival's land, and it simply wandered further than planned.
The creature is someone's escaped pet, bought from a smuggler, and the owner will pay double to have it back quietly.
The livestock losses are exaggerated; the farmer is using the hunt to cover up selling his own sheep.
A village child has been feeding the monster, and it now treats that child as part of its pack.
The monster is not the one killing livestock; a second, quieter predator is, and it has been letting the first take the blame.
The creature is guarding an unhatched clutch that, if left, will become a far worse problem in spring.
A rival house paid a beast-handler to drive the monster here to ruin the client's harvest.
The monster was once a druid's companion, and the druid wants it back alive and is willing to fight for it.
Killing the monster frees the spirit of something it ate, and that spirit has a request.
The reward is paid in spirit coins the client stole from the Adventure Society's own strongbox.
The monster is an escaped test subject from a Magic Society holding pen, and the Society wants this kept quiet.

details: The package is exactly what the client says it is, but a gang of thieves in {place} has been tipped off about its value.
The recipient moved a week ago and left no forwarding address; a DC 13 Charisma (Investigation or Persuasion) check around town finds them.
The road passes through a stretch of marsh where the causeway is flooded; crossing takes an extra day or a DC 12 Strength (Athletics) check per person.
The cargo is fragile and alive; it must be fed twice a day and kept warm at night.
The client hired two teams secretly and will pay only the first to arrive.
A customs post on the route demands a toll and an inspection of all cargo.
The package is heavier than its size suggests, and it shifts its weight on its own at night.
The recipient moved last week; the neighbours know where, but they want a favour first.
The road is quick but crosses a toll bridge whose keeper hates the client.
A second courier was sent with an identical package; only one of them is real.
The item is fragile: any fall of more than a few feet, or any failed DC 12 Dexterity save in a fight, cracks it.
The cargo draws monsters with its smell, so every night camp has a higher chance of an encounter.
The delivery comes with a letter to be read aloud to the recipient, and it is not good news.
The client's instructions include a password, and nobody told the recipient what it is.
Half the payment waits at the far end, with a recipient who has no money.
complications: The package grows heavier each day, and by the third day it takes two people to carry.
A storm forces the team to shelter in an inn whose owner is very curious about their cargo.
A desperate family on the road begs the team to share what they are carrying.
The seal cracks on the first night through no fault of the team, and the client will assume they opened it.
Bandits ambush the team at a river ford; {count} of them, poorly armed but desperate.
The recipient refuses delivery and claims never to have ordered it.
A customs post on the way insists on inspecting the cargo, and the client said no one may.
Bandits have word of a valuable shipment, though they have the wrong team in mind.
Heavy rain makes the shorter route impassable; the long way adds two days.
The cargo starts leaking something that smells like rotten eggs and burns leather.
A child stows away in the cart and refuses to say where they came from.
Someone offers the team three times the fee to hand the cargo over instead.
The recipient insists the item was damaged on the way and refuses to pay.
A road warden recognises the cargo as stolen goods from a theft last year.
One of the pack animals is lame and slows the team to half speed.
twists: The item is stolen property, and the team is unknowingly acting as fences for a smuggling ring.
The recipient is dead, and the person waiting to collect it is an impostor wearing their name.
The package contains a tracking charm, and the client is using the delivery to find a hidden enemy.
The cargo is a decoy; the real valuable is sewn into the lining of the satchel the team was given.
The sender and recipient are estranged lovers, and the delivery is a final message neither will admit to.
The item is a monster egg, and it hatches a day before arrival.
The recipient is dead, and their heir is someone the client would never send anything to.
The package contains evidence that would ruin the client, and the recipient intends to use it.
The cargo is a bribe intended for a Society official, which makes the team accomplices.
The item is cursed to return to its first owner, and that owner is waiting at the destination.
The delivery was a test of the team's honesty arranged by a noble house looking for agents.
The real cargo is a person hidden in the cart, escaping from something.
proof: A signed receipt from the named recipient
The recipient's wax seal on the Society delivery form
Return of the empty courier satchel with the client's token inside
A receipt signed and sealed by the recipient
The empty courier satchel, returned with the recipient's mark
A word-perfect message from the recipient, repeated back to the client

details: The caravan leader is overloaded and has refused to hire enough guards; the wagons move slowly and break axles.
The escorted person is a minor celebrity, and crowds slow travel through every village along the way.
The route passes a pass known for rockslides; a DC 13 Wisdom (Perception) check spots loose stone before it falls.
The client wants to travel at night to avoid attention, which means more monsters and less visibility.
One wagon carries undeclared goods that the client will not discuss.
The escorted group includes small children and a goat that wanders off at every stop.
The client insists on travelling only by daylight, which adds a day each way.
One of the wagons carries far more weight than its declared cargo of linen.
The escorted party includes an elderly scholar who wanders off whenever something catches her eye.
The client has hired a second, cheaper guard who resents the team and cuts corners.
The route passes a village that owes the client money and blames them for a bad harvest.
The client brings a menagerie of exotic pets, one of which escapes each night.
The road passes an astral space that has just opened, and its monsters hunt at dusk.
There are three possible routes; the client chooses the one with the best inn.
The client's servants know far more about the danger than the client does, and only talk when he's out of earshot.
complications: The person being escorted keeps slipping away at night to meet someone.
{faction} has placed a spy among the caravan's hired drivers.
Halfway through, the client changes the destination and demands the team keep going.
A bridge on the route has collapsed, adding two days through monster territory.
A pack of {count} {monster} shadows the group for days, waiting for stragglers.
The escorted person is allergic to most healing potions.
A bridge is out, and the only ford is guarded by a toll gang.
The client falls sick halfway and has to be carried.
A rival merchant train is on the same road and keeps racing to the next inn first.
A noble demands that the caravan give way, and refuses to move.
The client changes the destination halfway there.
An adventurer from the client's past turns up and wants the client dead.
A wagon wheel breaks in the worst possible place.
Half the pilgrims, or passengers, or animals decide to turn back.
A sudden fog makes it impossible to tell friend from foe on the road.

The bride does not want to marry and will try to bribe the team to lose her on the road.
The prisoner is innocent and the magistrate at the destination is the true criminal.
The caravan carries refugees hidden in false-bottomed wagons, and the people hunting them are law officers.
The person being escorted is an impostor, and the real one is already dead.
The client is smuggling a cultist out of the city under the team's protection.
The attackers are the client's own family, trying to stop a ruinous marriage.
The escorted wagon is bait; the real cargo went by another road with no guard.
The client is fleeing a debt owed to a crime boss who has hired another adventuring team.

The person being escorted is a hidden outworlder trying to reach someone who can help.
